title: Tax Benefits under Section 80D & Section 80C (Income Tax Act)
questions: How much tax can I save on health insurance under Section 80D?
What is the maximum limit under Section 80C?
Can I claim tax deduction for parents' health insurance?
What is the tax deduction for preventive health check-ups?
content: Key tax deductions under the Income Tax Act 1961 (applicable under the Old Tax Regime): (1) Section 80D (Health Insurance): Deductions up to ₹25,000 for self, spouse, and dependent children (<60 years). Additional ₹25,000 for parents (<60 years), or ₹50,000 if parents are senior citizens (≥60 years). Maximum combined deduction: ₹1,00,000 (if both self and parents are senior citizens). Includes up to ₹5,000 for preventive health check-ups within the overall cap. (2) Section 80C (Investments & Life Insurance): Up to ₹1,50,000 deduction for EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance premium (premium ≤ 10% of sum assured), home loan principal repayment, SSY, and children's tuition fees.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 80C & Section 80D Statutory Provisions

title: Old Tax Regime vs New Tax Regime: Slabs, Deductions & Section 115BAC Comparison
questions: What is the difference between Old and New Tax Regime?
Which tax regime is better for me in India?
What deductions are allowed in the New Tax Regime?
What is the standard deduction for salaried employees under the New Tax Regime?
content: Comparative analysis of dual personal tax systems under Section 115BAC: (1) New Tax Regime (Default): Features lower, streamlined slab rates (Nil up to ₹3L, 5% for ₹3-7L, 10% for ₹7-10L, 15% for ₹10-12L, 20% for ₹12-15L, 30% above ₹15L). Permits standard deduction of ₹75,000 for salaried employees and employer NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2), but disallows Chapter VI-A deductions (80C, 80D, HRA, home loan interest). (2) Old Tax Regime: Higher slab rates, but permits all deductions (80C up to ₹1.5L, 80D up to ₹1L, HRA, home loan interest up to ₹2L). (3) Choice Rule: Beneficial to switch to Old Regime only if total deductions exceed ~₹3.75 Lakh.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 115BAC & Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 Amendments

title: Section 87A Tax Rebate: Full Tax Exemption up to ₹7 Lakh in New Tax Regime
questions: Is income up to ₹7 Lakh tax-free in India?
How does Section 87A rebate work in the New Tax Regime?
What is marginal relief under Section 87A?
What is the maximum tax rebate under Section 87A in Old vs New regime?
content: Statutory tax relief provided to middle-income resident individuals under Section 87A: (1) New Tax Regime: Resident individuals with taxable income up to ₹7,00,000 receive a full tax rebate of up to ₹25,000, bringing their net income tax payable to exactly ₹0. (With the ₹75,000 standard deduction, salaried employees pay zero tax up to ₹7.75 Lakh gross income). (2) Marginal Relief: Introduced so individuals earning slightly above ₹7 Lakh do not pay tax that exceeds their incremental income. (3) Old Tax Regime: Rebate capped at ₹12,500 for total income up to ₹5,00,000.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 87A & CBDT Clarifications

title: Section 80CCD(1B): Exclusive ₹50,000 Tax Deduction for National Pension System
questions: How much extra tax can I save by investing in NPS?
What is Section 80CCD(1B) in income tax?
Is the ₹50,000 NPS deduction over and above the ₹1.5 Lakh 80C limit?
What is Section 80CCD(2) employer contribution deduction?
content: Special income-tax incentives encouraging retirement savings through the National Pension System (NPS Tier-1): (1) Section 80CCD(1B): An exclusive, independent tax deduction of up to ₹50,000 for individual voluntary contributions to NPS Tier-1. This ₹50,000 deduction is OVER AND ABOVE the standard ₹1,50,000 limit available under Section 80C, allowing up to ₹2,00,000 in total deductions. (2) Section 80CCD(2): Employer contribution to an employee's NPS (up to 10% of Basic + DA, or 14% for Central Government employees) is fully deductible in BOTH the Old and New Tax Regimes.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 80CCD & PFRDA Tax Guidelines

title: Section 10(10D): Life Insurance Maturity Taxability & ₹5 Lakh Premium Ceiling
questions: Is life insurance maturity payout tax-free in India?
What is the new ₹5 Lakh annual premium limit under Section 10(10D)?
Are ULIP maturity proceeds taxable?
Is death claim payout always tax-free for the nominee?
content: Rules governing tax exemption of life insurance proceeds under Section 10(10D): (1) Death Benefit: Sum received upon the DEATH of the insured is ALWAYS 100% tax-free for the nominee under all circumstances, without any monetary ceiling. (2) Maturity Taxability for Traditional Policies: For policies issued on or after April 1, 2023, if aggregate annual premium across non-linked policies exceeds ₹5,00,000, maturity proceeds are NOT exempt from tax; the gain component is taxed as income from other sources. (3) ULIP Cap: Policies issued after Feb 1, 2021 with annual premiums exceeding ₹2,50,000 are taxed as capital gains.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 10(10D) & CBDT Circular No. 15/2023

title: Capital Gains on Real Estate: 12.5% Tax & Section 54/54EC Capital Gains Bonds
questions: What is the capital gains tax on selling property in India after 2024?
How can I save tax on property sale under Section 54?
What are Section 54EC capital gains bonds (54EC bonds)?
How much money can be invested in 54EC bonds to save tax?
content: Taxation on property sales following Finance (No. 2) Act 2024: (1) Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG, held > 24 months): Taxed at 12.5% without indexation (properties acquired before July 23, 2024 retain an option to compute tax at 20% with indexation if beneficial). (2) Section 54 Exemption: Tax on LTCG from selling a residential house can be 100% exempted if gains are reinvested into purchasing another residential house within 1 year before or 2 years after sale (or constructing within 3 years). (3) Section 54EC Bonds: Invest LTCG up to ₹50,00,000 in REC, PFC, NHAI, or IRFC bonds within 6 months of sale (5-year lock-in).
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Sections 48, 54, 54EC & CBDT Notifications

title: Advance Tax Mandate: 15% - 45% - 75% - 100% Instalment Deadlines & Section 234B/C
questions: Who is required to pay advance tax in India?
What are the 4 instalment due dates for advance tax?
What is the penalty interest for paying advance tax late?
Are senior citizens exempt from advance tax?
content: Pay-as-you-earn tax compliance mandate under Section 208 of the Income Tax Act: (1) Liability Threshold: Every individual whose estimated net income-tax liability for the financial year (after deducting TDS/TCS) is ₹10,000 or more must pay advance tax. (2) Instalment Calendar: 15% on or before June 15; 45% on or before September 15; 75% on or before December 15; 100% on or before March 15. (3) Penal Interest: Delay or default attracts mandatory penal interest under Section 234B and 234C at 1% per month. (4) Exemption: Resident senior citizens (aged 60+) having no business/professional income are completely exempt.

title: Form 26AS, Annual Information Statement (AIS) & Tax Information Summary (TIS)
questions: What is the difference between Form 26AS and AIS (Annual Information Statement)?
How do I check TDS deducted by my employer or bank?
What high-value transactions appear in AIS?
What should I do if there is wrong information in my AIS?
content: Digital tax intelligence repositories maintained on the e-filing portal: (1) Form 26AS: Consolidated tax credit statement showing TDS deducted by employers/banks, TCS collected, advance tax paid, and self-assessment tax credits. (2) AIS (Annual Information Statement): Comprehensive financial dossier tracking 50+ data heads—including stock dividends, mutual fund sales, foreign remittances, cash deposits, property registrations, credit card bill payments > ₹10 Lakh. (3) TIS (Tax Information Summary): Summarized taxable values derived from AIS. (4) Feedback Loop: Taxpayers can submit online feedback in AIS disputing erroneous figures.
source: Income Tax Rules 1962 Rule 114-I & CBDT Guidelines on AIS

title: Income Tax Return Forms Guide: Choosing Between ITR-1, ITR-2, ITR-3, and ITR-4
questions: Which ITR form should I file?
Can I file ITR-1 if I have capital gains from shares or mutual funds?
What is ITR-4 Sugam for presumptive taxation?
What happens if I file the wrong ITR form?
content: Navigating statutory return filing categories under CBDT rules: (1) ITR-1 (Sahaj): For resident individuals with total income up to ₹50 Lakh from Salary, one house property, and other sources (interest). CANNOT be used if you have capital gains, business income, or foreign assets. (2) ITR-2: For individuals/HUFs having capital gains (shares, mutual funds, real estate), more than one house property, or foreign assets, but NO business/professional income. (3) ITR-3: For individuals with business or professional income. (4) ITR-4 (Sugam): For presumptive business income under Section 44AD/44ADA. Wrong form selection triggers a 'Defective Return' notice under Section 139(9).
source: CBDT Annual Notifications on Income Tax Return Forms

title: Belated and Revised ITR Filing under Section 139(4) & 139(5): Deadlines and Penalties
questions: What is the last date to file a belated tax return in India?
What is the penalty for filing ITR after July 31?
How many times can I revise my Income Tax Return?
Can I carry forward business or stock losses if I file late?
content: Statutory timelines and consequences under Section 139: (1) Original Due Date: July 31 of the assessment year for non-audit individuals. (2) Belated Return (Section 139(4)): Can be filed up to December 31 of the assessment year, subject to late filing fees under Section 234F (₹5,000 for income > ₹5 Lakh; ₹1,000 for income ≤ ₹5 Lakh) and loss of the right to carry forward capital/business losses. (3) Revised Return (Section 139(5)): Can be filed up to December 31 to rectify genuine errors or omissions discovered in an originally filed return, without any penalty.

title: Savings & FD Interest Deductions: Section 80TTA (₹10,000) vs Section 80TTB (₹50,000)
questions: Is savings bank interest tax-free up to ₹10,000 under Section 80TTA?
Does Section 80TTA apply to fixed deposit interest?
What is Section 80TTB deduction for senior citizens?
Can senior citizens claim both 80TTA and 80TTB?
content: Specific tax deductions for bank interest income: (1) Section 80TTA: Available to individuals aged below 60 and HUFs. Grants deduction up to ₹10,000 per financial year on interest earned exclusively from SAVINGS bank accounts (commercial banks, cooperative banks, post office). Does NOT apply to fixed deposits or recurring deposits. (2) Section 80TTB: Available exclusively to resident Senior Citizens (aged 60+). Grants deduction up to ₹50,000 per financial year across ALL bank deposits combined—including savings accounts, fixed deposits, and recurring deposits. Senior citizens cannot claim 80TTA.

title: Section 80G Deductions: 50% vs 100% Tax Relief for Registered Charitable Donations
questions: How much tax deduction do I get for charitable donations under Section 80G?
What is Form 10BE donation certificate?
Can I claim 80G deduction for cash donations?
Which donations qualify for 100% tax deduction without qualifying limits?
content: Rules governing charitable donation deductions under Section 80G: (1) Deduction Categories: (a) 100% deduction without qualifying limit: National Defence Fund, Prime Minister's National Relief Fund, PM CARES Fund. (b) 50% deduction without limit: Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund. (c) 50% or 100% deduction subject to a qualifying limit (10% of Adjusted Gross Total Income) for approved religious trusts, educational institutions, and NGOs. (2) Form 10BE Mandate: Taxpayers must obtain a formal donation certificate in Form 10BE generated by the NGO. (3) Cash Limit: Cash donations exceeding ₹2,000 are completely disallowed.
source: Income Tax Act 1961 Section 80G & CBDT Rules on Charitable Trusts
